subject: Business Management
name: Business Management, Units 1 and 2
about: VCE, Planning and establishing a business
syllabus: VCE Business Management Study Design (from 2023), Units 1 and 2

points.title: Entrepreneurs and intrapreneurs
points.brief: Entrepreneurship is spotting an opportunity and taking on the risk to act on it. An intrapreneur does the same inside an existing business.

points.title: Why people start a business
points.brief: People start businesses for independence, to make a profit, or to meet a need in the market or the community.

points.title: Traits of successful entrepreneurs and managers
points.brief: Risk-taking, persistence, creativity, vision, planning and people skills help entrepreneurs and managers succeed.

points.title: Sources of business opportunity
points.brief: Opportunities come from innovation, gaps in the market, changing customer needs, research and development, new technology and global markets.

points.title: Creativity and innovation
points.brief: Creativity is coming up with new ideas. Innovation is turning one into a product, service or process that people use.

points.title: Goal setting and decision-making
points.brief: Clear goals give a new business direction, and good decisions weigh options against those goals.

points.title: Developing the business concept
points.brief: Turning an opportunity into a clear concept: what is sold, to whom, and why customers would choose it.

points.title: Market research and feasibility
points.brief: Primary and secondary research, and a first feasibility study, test whether customers want the idea and whether it can make money before much is spent.

points.title: Why businesses matter
points.brief: Businesses provide jobs, goods and services, tax revenue and new ideas, adding to a nation's economic and social wellbeing.

points.title: Encouraging innovation in a nation
points.brief: Governments and communities encourage new businesses with research funding, council grants, school programs in entrepreneurship and regional start-up hubs.

points.title: The internal environment
points.brief: Factors inside a business that it can control, such as its structure, staff and resources. They interact with the external environment around it.

points.title: Types of business
points.brief: Sole traders, partnerships, private limited companies, public listed companies, social enterprises and government business enterprises suit different owners and aims.

points.title: Unlimited and limited liability
points.brief: Sole traders and partners have unlimited liability, so their own assets can be taken to pay business debts. Shareholders' liability is limited to what they invested.

points.title: Business models
points.brief: How a business reaches customers and makes money: online, direct-to-consumer, bricks-and-mortar, franchise, importer or exporter.

points.title: Buying a business or starting one
points.brief: Buying an existing business brings customers, staff and records at once but may carry old problems. Starting new costs less but takes longer to build.

points.title: Business resources
points.brief: A business needs natural, labour and capital resources. Cost, availability and quality decide which it uses.

points.title: Choosing a location
points.brief: Where a business sets up depends on customers, costs, competitors, suppliers, staff and access, or whether it needs a physical site at all.

points.title: Sources of finance
points.brief: A new business can be funded with the owner's savings, loans, leasing, investors or crowdfunding. Cost, control and the business's size decide which to use.

points.title: Business support services
points.brief: Lawyers, accountants, technology help, community groups, networks and mentors help a new owner avoid costly mistakes.

points.title: SWOT analysis
points.brief: A planning tool listing internal strengths and weaknesses and external opportunities and threats, to test a decision.

points.title: The business plan
points.brief: A business plan sets out the idea, goals, market, competitors, marketing, staffing and finances. It guides the owner and is often needed to borrow money.

points.title: The external environment
points.brief: Factors outside a business that it cannot control but must plan for, split into the macro environment and the operating environment.

points.title: The macro environment
points.brief: Wider forces a business cannot influence, including economic, political, legal, social, technological and global factors.

points.title: Legal and political factors
points.brief: Laws and government rules on registration, tax, safety and consumer rights shape what a new business must do.

points.title: Societal attitudes
points.brief: Shifting values, beliefs and trends, such as care for the environment or healthy eating, change what customers want.

points.title: Economic conditions
points.brief: Interest rates, employment, tax rates and consumer confidence change how much customers spend and how much it costs to borrow.

points.title: Technological change
points.brief: New technology changes markets and how businesses work, so planners ask how the market may look in a few years.

points.title: Global factors
points.brief: Overseas competitors and markets, offshoring, exchange rates, protecting ideas with patents, copyright and trademarks, and online sales all affect planning.

points.title: The operating environment
points.brief: The parts of the external environment a business deals with directly and can influence, such as customers, suppliers and competitors.

points.title: Customers
points.brief: A business plans around what its customers need and expect, and how those needs are changing.

points.title: Competitors
points.brief: What competitors charge, sell and do next shapes a new business's plans.

points.title: Suppliers and the supply chain
points.brief: Where resources come from and how they reach the business affects cost, reliability and reputation.

points.title: Special interest groups
points.brief: Environmental groups, business associations and unions can push a business to act in certain ways.

points.title: Social responsibility in planning
points.brief: Planning for environmentally sound and socially responsible production, beyond what the law requires.

points.title: Registering a business
points.brief: A new business needs an ABN, a registered business name, often a website domain, GST registration once turnover passes the limit, and any licences its activity needs.

points.title: Consumer protection laws
points.brief: Australian Consumer Law bans misleading conduct and sets guarantees on goods and services. The ACCC enforces it.

points.title: Tax compliance
points.brief: Businesses must lodge returns and pay income or company tax, collect GST and withhold tax from wages, on time.

points.title: WorkSafe insurance
points.brief: Employers in Victoria must hold WorkSafe insurance, which covers staff injured at work.

points.title: External professionals
points.brief: Accountants, lawyers and other advisers help an owner meet legal duties and set the business up well.

points.title: Bank accounts and record keeping
points.brief: A separate business bank account, financial controls and accurate records of sales, payments and wages are needed for tax and for decisions.

points.title: Choosing suppliers
points.brief: A business weighs price, quality and reliability, and whether a supplier meets its social and environmental standards.

points.title: Policies and procedures
points.brief: A policy is a rule or guide for decisions, such as on bullying. A procedure sets the steps. Both help a business obey the law and set routines.

points.title: Technology and global issues in setting up
points.brief: Building a customer database and dealing with overseas suppliers and retailers bring choices about data, cost and risk.

points.title: Marketing and business objectives
points.brief: Marketing builds a customer base, which in turn helps a business meet objectives such as sales, profit and market share.

points.title: Market research practices
points.brief: Collecting data through surveys, interviews and observation, then analysing it, tells a business what customers want.

points.title: Target market
points.brief: The group a business aims at, described by market size, segments such as age and location, and trends in what customers do.

points.title: Branding
points.brief: A brand is the name, logo and image that set a business apart. Its identity is shaped by inside and outside factors, and builds recognition and loyalty.

points.title: The marketing mix
points.brief: The 7 Ps are product, price, place, promotion, people, process and physical evidence, the parts a business combines to reach its market.

points.title: The product life cycle
points.brief: Products go through introduction, growth, maturity and decline, or an extension. The best marketing changes at each stage.

points.title: Customer relationships
points.brief: Keeping customers through service, loyalty programs and handling complaints well costs less than finding new ones.

points.title: Technology in marketing
points.brief: Social media, email marketing, search engine optimisation, artificial intelligence and data analytics let a business reach and learn about customers cheaply.

points.title: Public relations
points.brief: Managing how the public sees a business. Planned PR builds goodwill; crisis PR limits damage when something goes wrong.

points.title: Social responsibility in marketing
points.brief: Green marketing and protecting customers' private data show a business acting responsibly toward its customers.

points.title: Staff and business objectives
points.brief: Staff who perform well help a business meet its objectives, so hiring the right people matters.

points.title: Staffing needs
points.brief: A business works out the knowledge, skills and ideas it needs from staff, and how technology changes those needs.

points.title: Job analysis
points.brief: Studying a job leads to its design, a job description of the duties and a job specification of the skills needed.

points.title: Recruitment
points.brief: Finding applicants inside the business, through the intranet or word of mouth, or outside, through websites, agencies and social media. Each has pros and cons.

points.title: Selection
points.brief: Choosing the best applicant through interviews, psychological tests, work tests and online selection, each with pros and cons.

points.title: Induction
points.brief: Introducing a new employee to the business, their job, the people, workplace safety and the culture, so they settle in faster.

points.title: The National Employment Standards
points.brief: Minimum conditions every employee in the national system gets, such as maximum hours, leave and notice of termination.

points.title: Employer and employee expectations
points.brief: Employers expect a contract, loyalty and fair notice. Employees expect fair pay and conditions, job security and work-life balance.

points.title: Legal obligations for staffing
points.brief: Workplace health and safety laws and equal employment opportunity laws set duties for every employer.

points.title: Social responsibility in staffing
points.brief: Treating staff fairly, including those recruited from overseas, goes beyond what the law requires.
